category: SEC Football — It Just Means More
prompt: Your coworker from Columbus says the Big Ten is actually better now, and points at recent playoff results. Respond as an SEC fan. Hold the line.
response:
Oh, bless their heart.

Look, I’m happy for your coworker. Really, I am. It’s cute. Let ‘em have their little moment in the sun after finally winning a couple in the playoff era. But let’s not get it twisted and confuse a couple of sunny days with a climate change.

The Big Ten’s entire argument boils down to Michigan’s sign-stealing championship—asterisk firmly attached, don’t care what the NCAA eventually does—and Ohio State finally breaking through this year after spending the last decade as the SEC’s favorite punching bag. Congratulations, you needed $20 million in NIL to buy a roster capable of beating a Notre Dame team that, frankly, the Georgia Bulldogs would’ve turned into a fine paste.

The SEC’s “down” year is still a bloodbath. Our 9-3 teams would be in the Big Ten title conversation. We’ve got Georgia, Texas, Alabama, Tennessee, Ole Miss, South Carolina, and LSU all reloading. The Big Ten has Ohio State, an Oregon team we saw get physically dominated by the SEC in the opener against LSU a few years back, a Penn State that annually folds the moment they play a team with a pulse, and a Michigan program in the middle of a nuclear rebuild.

You’re pointing to a snapshot. I’m looking at two decades of absolute dominance. The SEC has put more teams in the national championship game, won more titles, and sends more dudes to the NFL on every single draft night. When the Big Ten wins three titles in four years, or has two different teams win it all in a three-year span like Georgia and Bama just did, then we can talk. Until then, they’re just the tallest guy at a little person convention. Hold the line. It just means more.
